newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch forecast higher growth, subdued inflation.
newsitem.headline: Dutch forecast higher growth, subdued inflation.

text.p: The Dutch government's central planning bureau (CPB) on Tuesday presented a rosy picture for the Dutch economy in a quarterly interim forecast.

Growth in gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to accelerate this year and in 1998, taking unemployment down to levels last seen more than a decade ago and supporting the public finances, but without stoking inflationary pressures.

The CPB increased its forecast for GDP growth in 1997 to 3.25 percent from a prior estimate of 3.0 percent given in April. In 1998, growth is seen rising to 3.75 percent as against a previous forecast of 3.25 percent.

The forecast expansion is particularly supported by expected rapid export growth stimulated by stronger world trade. The CPB sees nonenergy export growth of 6.25 percent in 1997 and 8.25 percent in 1998.

The figures are distorted by the effect of the current swine fever outbreak in the south of the country, without which export growth would have been between seven and 7.5 percent in both years, the bureau said.
The increased GDP growth will, despite a considerable increase in the labour supply, see the unemployment rate dropping to six percent in 1998, the lowest level since the early 1980s, the CPB said.
However, the bureau said there was little sign of tightness in the labour market as yet and held to its previous two percent forecast for Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation in 1998.
On the basis of better-than-expected actual data so far this year, the bureau cut its 1997 inflation forecast by half a percent to 2.25 percent.
With growth accelerating, the Netherlands' public finances are seen showing further improvement.

The Dutch public sector deficit is seen at two percent of GDP in 1997 and the CPB said indications were, given some technical assumptions about the 1998 budget, that this would shrink to 1.75 percent of GDP in 1998.
The Public sector debt/GDP ratio was "plummeting", the CPB said, seen at 73.5 percent in 1997 and around 71.5 percent in 1998, from 79.7 percent in 1995.
"The Dutch economy is in good shape," the CPB said. "The Netherlands remains an economic front runner in Europe."
